## Introduction

The USFS Forest Inventory and Analysis (FIA) Program surveys and analyzes the forests of the
United States through a nationwide network of 
permanent sample locations. These plot locations are distributed across all lands with a spatial 
sampling intensity of about 1 location per 2400 ha according to an 
unaligned, quasi-systematic equal probability sample design. This design 
is spatially dispersed with deviation from a regular grid 
to avoid alignment of sample locations with periodic population features.
Statistical inference on forest population 
status and change parameters is enabled by measurements of forest
vegetation traits made at these locations by field crews. 

Historically, FIA sample locations in each state were visited periodically 
as time, budgets, and workforce capacity allowed. This approach offered 
logistical flexibility but complicated analysis and reporting timelines.
In the early 2000's the program shifted 
from periodic to annual inventory protocols calling for approximately equal 
numbers of plot measurements each year on schedules
intended to be fixed and consistent within states.
Under this annual inventory, each 
plot location in a state is assigned to one of a set of panels, 
and all plot locations assigned to a panel are designated for measurement in the 
same year. The panels in a state together comprise an inventory cycle, and 
inventory cycles range in length from 5 or 7 years in the eastern US to 10 years in the west.
Once the final panel in an inventory 
cycle is complete, remeasurements at sample locations in the first panel begin the following year. 
For more information regarding the FIA sample design see [@gb1; @gb2 Chapter 2].

In general, FIA requires that a panel be complete before the associated tabular
data are pushed to its public-facing databases, which the program endeavors to do
within 1 year of panel completion. Similarly, FIA requires a complete inventory cycle 
within a state to publish official state-scale estimates 
of forest parameters in fulfillment of 
Congressional reporting obligations. In practice, however,
adherence to the annual design described above has proven very challenging or
impossible for the FIA Program. Instead, delayed and skipped field measurements 
cause unintentional lengthening of inventory cycles
and/or survey nonresponse [see, e.g., @sarndal_nonresponse], 
at rates that vary regionally and over time. 

The underlying causes 
of delayed and skipped field measurements are varied, and can be chronic 
(e.g., denied access to private lands [@westfall2022spatial], 
logistical or administrative challenges in remote regions [@affleck2026inventory], 
persistent workforce and budgetary constraints [@conroy_thesis]) 
or can result from discrete events (e.g., the COVID19 pandemic [@covid]). 
Late measurements of temporally dynamic variables can induce a "time lag" bias
in point estimates when the time component of the estimand is not adjusted accordkingly.
Further, survey nonresponse can introduce nonresponse bias to estimates
of population parameters when response propensity is correlated with the attribute 
of interest. 
Better understanding of patterns
in late and skipped measurements [@conroy_thesis], 
and the investigation of new sampling and estimation techniques
to ameliorate the statistical consequences of nonresponse [@westfall2022estimation; 
@westfall2026double] are active research
topics, but beyond the scope of the present study. 

Of immediate practical concern for FIA and its external partners are the strain on 
field staff and delays to tabular data publication that result from delayed 
field measurements. Methods have been proposed to control the measurement delay 
process by disaggregating FIA’s annual panel structure into subpanels while still preserving the spatial 
dispersion of the FIA sample network within field season
years. Disaggregation of panels into subpanels enables intentional alignment of workloads with anticipated data 
acquisition workforce capacity in each field season year through the application of variable
annual field sampling effort within individual states.  

Though the logistical advantages of variable annual effort (VAE) are profound (i.e., it can help 
ensure the long-term viability of the inventory in the context of funding and staffing 
volatility), the statistical consequences of the redistribution of partial 
panels within inventory cycles, and of extended and variable inventory cycle lengths, are 
unknown across states and 
epochs. In particular, a need exists to understand and communicate to stakeholders how 
adoption of VAE protocols may influence the statistical properties of forest parameter estimates 
published by FIA in fulfillment of Congressional reporting imperatives.  

Therefore, our research objectives in this study are to:

1. define three VAE regimens with respect to subpanels 
(fast and slow start, dropped subpanels, and extended 
and shortened cycle lengths) intended to be representative of circumstances FIA could
conceivably encounter in program administration
2. simulate the influence of those three VAE regimens on state-scale, inventory-cycle wide
estimates of total net merchantable timber volume for three US states with distinct
forest types, ecological attributes, and FIA inventory cycle lengths.
3. visualize and discuss simulation results in the context of implications for 
FIA program operations and the management of US forests.
